Human beings and humanity are therefore necessarily also antithetical.
And everything specifically human in the human being is contained in this antithetical character.
What, then, is a human being as antithesis?
“The [human] individual is in himself and for himself: he is for himself, or [in other words] he is a free activity (Tun).”
Insofar as the human being exists “in himself and for himself”—that is, insofar as he is dialectical or synthetic—he must also necessarily exist as antithesis.
And to exist as negation means to “exist for oneself”: ultimately, to be self-conscious.
For Hegel, this amounts to the same thing as being a “free activity,” or, in a word, being free.
We can now see why the human being is specifically human only as antithesis—or as a synthesis containing antithesis.
Outside self-consciousness and freedom, there is no properly human existence.

And conversely, there is neither freedom nor self-consciousness outside human existence, since we do not recognize the existence of “angels” or “gods,” which, as we will see, are incompatible with free self-consciousness or self-conscious human freedom.
The negativity that dominates the antithesis is therefore nothing other than human freedom.

And the realization of negativity—that is, the realization of dialectic itself—is nothing other than the realization of this freedom: what Hegel calls the carrying out of free activity, or action (Tat).

Human freedom is not realized in thought or in speech (logos). It is realized through action in the direct and full sense of the word—ultimately, as we will later discover, through physical work and bloody struggle.
But for an action to be genuinely free—that is, antithetical, and therefore also dialectical or human—it must be “negative,” or more precisely, negating.
Human freedom is certainly not “freedom of choice” (liberum arbitrium), as people have often believed and as some bourgeois thinkers still do.
When a person chooses between two things already “given,” he is not free at all. Many philosophers understood this long before Hegel—Spinoza, for example.
A person chooses whichever option seems “better” to him.
He is therefore fully “determined” by what seems better.
And what seems better to him does so because of the relation connecting him with everything that exists—a relation “given” to him just as the existing world itself is given.
Ultimately, then, it is the existing world that “chooses” within him, not the person himself.
Insofar as a human being exists, he is necessarily “determined” by everything that exists: by the whole natural and historical world.
To use Spinoza’s excellent comparison, a person chooses his path through the world in exactly the same way that a stone rolling down a mountain chooses its path.
In a word, it only seems to him that he chooses freely.
Authentic freedom can also, if we like, be called a “choice.”
But it is a choice between what exists and what does not exist.
Freedom is the choice of what is not.
For what does not exist cannot determine anyone, for the simple reason that it does not exist.
The choice of what does not exist is therefore determined not by what is chosen, but by the one who chooses.
And that is precisely what it means for the choice to be free or “spontaneous.”
But choosing what does not exist is not really a “choice” in the ordinary sense.
It is rather the determinate negation of what exists.
We can therefore say that the real and authentic freedom of the human being is nothing other than his negativity, or his antithetical character.
By choosing what does not yet exist, the human being introduces something new into what already exists.
But what he has chosen is, for the moment, still nothing.
To introduce something genuinely new, he must somehow transform this chosen nothing into something. He must realize it.
And to realize what does not yet exist is what we call action—action in the strong sense of the word: creative action.
We can therefore say that freedom is realized only through creative action, and that every genuinely creative action is free.

But what does not exist cannot exist separately before its realization, since by definition it is still nothing. Before being realized, it can be present only by “leaning on” what already exists and being related to it.
That means it can be present only as the negation of what exists.
To realize freedom, then, is nothing other than to realize “negativity”: to negate some identity or thesis, whether natural or human, historical—both outside the human being and within him.
In other words, the realization of freedom is always revolutionary.
Every revolution realizes freedom in some way.
An action is free insofar as it is creative.
And it is creative insofar as it is revolutionary—that is, insofar as it negates something “given.”

Conversely, the revolutionary negation of the given is always free, because what is “given” tends only to preserve itself. And it is always creative or innovative because, by realizing itself, it changes the given: it introduces into it something that was not there before.

This is why the dialectical—and therefore antithetical—understanding of the human being can be expressed in Bakunin’s remarkable “dialectical” formula, which comes ultimately from Hegel and which every genuine revolutionary understands and makes his own:
“The spirit of destruction is a spirit of creation.”

But if the dialectical—that is, antithetical and therefore human—character of the human being is genuinely essential, then human action, revolutionary and creative negation, must affect the person’s essential qualities.
In other words, a human being must be capable of changing his own “essence” or “nature”—his “given being”—while still remaining himself.
This is precisely why we can say that the human being is dialectical and human, that is, free.
And he is free only insofar as he possesses no eternal and unchanging “nature”—or at least insofar as, when he acts, he is not bound by such a nature.

In philosophical language, the human being is free insofar as he is transcendent: insofar as he “goes beyond” his own limits, overcomes himself as something “given” and conditioned by his “place” in the cosmos, and makes or creates himself as a free being through the revolutionary negation of what has been externally determined and imposed on him.
In religious language, we could say that the human being is free insofar as he is capable of conversion.

If he is capable of essentially “transforming” himself, he can turn from a subject completely “determined” by his place in the natural and historical world—from someone passively obedient to what is and to what is “given” to him—into a revolutionary who actively negates that “given.”
And in doing so he also negates himself, insofar as he forms part of that given world: insofar as he is merely the “son of his father,” the “representative of his class,” the “man of his time.”
The realization of freedom therefore seems to split the human being in two.
By negating himself as something “given,” he opposes himself to himself. He thereby exists for himself—in other words, he exists consciously.

So if we say that “the human being is human—that is, different from an animal—simply because he possesses self-consciousness,” we must now add that this self-consciousness necessarily presupposes self-negation: creative action, the realization of freedom, and therefore a certain revolutionary character.
It is only after a revolution, through the revolution and because of it, that we can fully understand what the “old regime” was and relate to it with full consciousness.
And what is true of political life is equally true of every other domain of human life.
The human being is human—that is, free and self-conscious—only because his existence includes the “moment” of antithesis.
But he can no more be only antithesis than he can be only thesis.
More precisely, if he were only thesis, he would certainly exist, but not as a human being. He would simply be an animal.
If, on the other hand, his existence were reduced entirely to antithesis, he would annihilate himself. He would turn, so to speak, into “pure” negation—that is, into nothing.
If the human being “were” nothing but negation, he would not be at all.
So insofar as he exists, and exists specifically as a human being, he must be simultaneously both thesis and antithesis.
And this means that he must be not merely thesis, and not merely antithesis, but a third thing as well:
We must therefore ask what the human being is as synthesis.
What is his synthetic aspect? What is the “moment” in which, as we already know, the category of totality predominates?
We know that synthesis appears as the result of antithesis, which itself presupposes thesis.
And we also know that antithesis reaches a positive or synthetic result because its negation is concrete: it is determined by the specific character of what it negates.
Non-A becomes some determinate B because it contains A within itself, preserves A, and is defined by it.
And this is exactly what happens in every “conversion.”
What a converted person becomes is determined by what he was before the conversion.

When a member of the thirteenth-century “gilded youth”—Francis of Assisi—is converted, the result is very different from what happens when the same thing occurs to a sixteenth-century Spanish soldier such as Ignatius of Loyola.

And when a minor French nobleman of the eighteenth century becomes a revolutionary—for example, Robespierre—the result is different from what happens when a minor Russian nobleman of the nineteenth century becomes one.
In the first case, the outcome includes “the sacred right of property”; in the second, its abolition.
More generally, the result of every revolution is in some way determined by the “old regime” it overthrows.
That old regime is therefore, in a certain sense, preserved within the revolution, although obviously in a transformed form.
And what is true of humanity as a whole is also true of every individual human being.
When a person negates himself, it is himself that he negates.
For that very reason, he remains identical with himself.
Even in his negation, he is determined by what he was before it.
This is why the result of a free action—that is, an antithetical or negating action—is always synthetic.

The past that is negated can be said to survive insofar as a person remembers it. The synthetic side of human existence therefore corresponds to memory (Erinnerung). Memory is what gives a personality its unity. If someone who had undergone a “conversion” completely forgot who they had been before, we could hardly say that we were dealing with one and the same person; we would really be dealing with two different individuals. And there is no doubt that the memory of the past enters into every revolution and helps determine its character. More generally, a real human being is never an “Ivan the Amnesiac”. Memories of the past—including the past one rejects—form an essential part of conscious, and therefore human, life. We simply have to understand “memory” here in a broad sense. Ordinary conscious recollection makes up only a small part of it. The past therefore often continues to operate in a person’s present without that person being aware of it.

We can also say that memory brings inside us what at first existed only outside us. The past exists only “inside” a consciousness that remembers it, not in the objective reality “outside” us. So when a person retains the memory of a thesis after having negated it in the antithesis, they internalize and make their own something that had previously been, in a certain sense, “dead” and external to them. What had existed “in itself” now exists “for them”: as their past, the past they know. Through memory, in this broad sense, a human being seems to absorb the past. The past lives in the human being just as the human being lives in the past. And in this sense the human being is genuinely total, because they contain everything that came before them.

But memory and knowledge of the past are nothing other than history. And any being that incorporates its past into its present existence, and can be defined by that past, is historical. We can therefore say that a human being is synthetic—that is, genuinely human—to the extent that they are historical.

But we must not forget that a person’s historical past, precisely because it is dialectical and human, necessarily contains an antithesis as well: a negation of what that past was and of what the person themselves once was. Human beings differ from animals, and are “more” than animals, only because they negate themselves—or at least can negate themselves. Yet they remain genuinely human, rather than becoming sheer nothingness, only because they remember what they have negated. It is only through this memory that they remain the same person who is being negated and the same person who performs the negation.
